reasoning: New PET (11C-PBR28, 18F-flortaucipir), MRI, arterial blood, genotyping and neuropathology data were collected from recruited participants (D1; available on request). Existing research software (PMOD v3.9, FreeSurfer 6.0.0, SPM12) was used for preprocessing, kinetic modelling and statistics; no new software is claimed (S2).

S1D1. S1 – The authors developed and released their own BEAMS implementation (“Our code is available online”, footnote 19; GitHub with example inputs; Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.572990). They also extended the GalSNID classifier to use host galaxy spectroscopy. Existing research software (CosmoMC, SNANA, PSNID, SALT2) is used too, but generated takes precedence. D1 – They ran a new spectroscopic follow-up survey (MMT/Hectospec, AAT, APO, WIYN), observing 3,930 host galaxies and obtaining 3,147 reliable redshifts, roughly 600 of which came from public surveys. They also generated large SNANA Monte Carlo simulations of the PS1 survey, which count as simulation outputs. The goal of the study being a methodology doesn’t change the grade, because new observational data was collected in the process.

S2D1. The study collects new data, including blood measurements, flow cytometry, IgG ELISA readings and PTPRC genotypes, which makes it D1. It analyses that data in R with the specialised packages mgcv (for the GAMs) and jtrans (for Johnson transformations). Those packages are named, versioned and central to the main results, which makes them research software that was used rather than generic utility software, so S2. This matches the S2D1 example of new measurements analysed with an established statistical package.

Software (S3): The paper doesn’t mention any software, research-specific or generic. The analysis was done by reading and interpreting texts.
Data (D3): The Research Method section describes a coding scheme the authors built while reading the bureaucracy literature, mainly Weber (1922) and Styhre (2007). They then matched its nine concepts to the Balanced Scorecard literature by Kaplan & Norton. So the only source material is published literature, and the criteria explicitly exclude “literature and papers” from research data. There are no interviews, surveys, case organisations or measurements.
Agreed.

S2D1. They use existing ML tools (Weka with default parameters, and the JADBio AutoML platform), and no authored software is described or credited in the contributions. They reuse their existing 192-patient adult autism assessment dataset (from [71]), but they also collect new questionnaire responses from 30 and 18 patients for the two new ASTA screening tools (Section 4), so the data is generated.

This paper develops a new energy management system for a small-scale PV-battery microgrid, which I’m treating as research software. The authors implemented it themselves: as a MATLAB script for the simulation work, and in the lab as LabVIEW with embedded MATLAB functions they wrote for load forecasting (ANFIS), PV forecasting and MILP optimisation, plus a real-time predictive controller with adaptive AR forecasting (S1). The research uses existing data (PV profiles from PVOutput.org, CREST load profiles and SODA weather data), but it also generates new research data. The authors made synthetic forecast profiles by adding noise (3.6% MAPE) to the real PV generation data. The experiments on the FlexElec lab microgrid also produced new measurements, including the battery’s state of charge and grid power recorded at a 1-minute sample time. Synthetic data and experimental measurements are both research data under the criteria (D1).

SPSS, Matlab and Adobe Audition are used only as utilities for processing and analysis, and no software is claimed as a contribution (S3). New field recordings, 360° videos and questionnaire responses from 120 participants are collected, and the dataset is deposited on Mendeley Data (D1).

Generates a new behavioural observation dataset (ethogram-based scoring from CCTV) → D1. Software used only as utilities: CCTV video management, Excel for data entry, and R for basic statistical tests → S3.

S3D2. The paper is a post-hoc secondary analysis of data from the Salt Substitute and Stroke Study (SSaSS), a cluster randomised trial. It uses that trial’s existing follow-up data and linked health insurance and mortality records to estimate the effect of salt substitutes on cancer outcomes. The results are rate ratios and confidence intervals calculated from this existing data. The paper does not claim to create a new dataset, so it counts as D2 (data used). The clinical coding and review of cancer events are described only as part of preparing the analysis, which isn’t clear enough evidence of data generation for D1. The only software named is SAS 9.4, which is generic statistical software and so not research software under the criteria. It was used as a utility for the statistical analysis, so it counts as S3. The data availability statement says analysis code can be requested, but the paper never presents that code as a contribution, so it doesn’t support S1.

S2: Uses existing research software (SPM12 with DCM10, FreeSurfer, FSL, 3D Slicer). No new software is claimed.

D1: The authors acquired new EEG-fMRI and MRI data in Modena under the study’s own ethics approval and consent, then derived the IED markers, BOLD maps and DCM results. The Data Availability statement confirms the datasets.
Agreed

S3D1. The paper doesn’t claim to have created or used any research software. The only mention, “design software to decide optimum path planning”, is in a list of recommended future actions, and proposed artefacts don’t count (S3). The proposed model was built from a review of the literature, which isn’t research data. However, the authors then validated it through two case studies they carried out themselves, at an automobile SME and a mining machinery assembly unit in India, and Section 4 cites no other studies. In both case studies they recorded their own shop-floor observations through Gemba walks, interviews and brainstorming sessions with staff. These include worker numbers, downtime, working time, production lead time, uptime and production per day (Tables 2–5). The Data Availability Statement also says “the data presented in this study are available on request.” This counts as new observational fieldwork data generated by the research (D1). It’s a weak D1, though: the dataset is small and summary-level, and the “improved condition” figures may be projected rather than measured.

D2 (data used). The whole analysis runs on the Russian Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS), using its 2002–2019 waves. That’s an existing panel survey run by the Carolina Population Center and HSE Moscow, which the authors didn’t collect. They do derive new variables from it: vulnerability lines, vulnerability gaps, spell-length dummies and deflated income. But the criteria say findings or statistics derived from a data source stay at D2, and the paper never presents these variables as a new dataset. So there’s no case for D1.

S3 (no software). I searched the full text and there’s no mention of any software: no Stata, R, Python, package names or code. The fixed-effects regressions must have been run in something, but under the criteria S3 applies when software isn’t claimed. Even if they named it, it would almost certainly be generic statistical software like Stata, which the criteria already exclude from research software.
Agreed

S2D1: The paper’s results come from a suite of numerical simulations of rotating convection in a spherical shell, so a research-specific simulation code is central to the work. This rules out S3. However, the paper does not claim to have created or significantly extended that code. The Methods cite the model to Willis et al. (2007), and the Code availability statement says the code “is described in Willis et al.” and is available on request. Without clear evidence of new development, the software is classed as used (S2). Visualisation tools (VisIt, Matplotlib, seaborn) are utilities only. For data, the authors run six new simulations and analyse 68 runs in total, including runs from their previous study. They derive temperature profiles and inversion-layer thicknesses from these outputs. Simulation outputs count as research data under the criteria, and the paper states that “the data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author on request”. This makes the data generated (D1). The paper also uses existing data (a seismic tomography model for the heat-flux pattern, and PREM), but generated data takes precedence over used data.

Analyses existing long-read structural-variant data from the NABEC cohort (dbGaP phs001300, provided by Billingsley/Blauwendraat), plus the hg38 reference, DGV and UniProt. No new dataset is claimed (D2). Uses established research software including RepeatMasker, BLAST, EMBOSS Transeq, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2 and FigTree. No new software is claimed (S2).
Agreeed

“No software (S3). The authors generate new observational data: they examine 233 sharks and report prevalence and intensity of infection, plus histological observations and images. Physical samples (the slides) are not data, but the data recorded from them is, and the Data Availability statement says this data is available on request (D1).”

Agreed. S2D1. The study isolates 44 new flavophages and generates new phage genome sequences and spring-bloom metagenomes, deposited at NCBI (PRJNA639310) (D1). Analysis relies on existing research software including VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, IQ-TREE and WIsH. Genome annotation used a previously published custom pipeline “with modifications”, but these are not claimed as a significant extension, so software is classed as used (S2).

Simulation study plus a real data application. Software: model fitting uses the research-specific ltm R package (p.271, rendered as ‘Itm’ in the PDF text), alongside R’s optim and NumDeriv (p.263), so this is S2. The authors’ own code isn’t claimed as a contribution, so not S1. Data: they analyse the existing Miller et al. (1984) dataset, so this is D2. The simulated data isn’t presented as an artefact, so not D1.

S1D1. The paper presents the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric as a software tool. It is freely available online, with a Software and Data Availability statement, two authors credited with the Software role, and co-ownership by the University of Cambridge. It was built under contract for the research, so the paper claims to have created research software: S1. The metric also generates new research data. Panels of experts (27 for temperate forest, 23 for Mediterranean and semi-arid) scored each action through expert judgement and a modified Delphi evidence assessment. Stakeholder workshops defined the action lists. The full set of resulting scores is provided as Supplementary Table S12. These elicited scores work as the metric’s weights and count as new research data, as do the survey-style expert responses. The Conservation Evidence database and one example farm’s outputs are existing data that was used, but generation takes priority: D1. The statement that “the data that has been used is confidential” doesn’t change the grade, because sharing is not part of the criteria.

S3D1. The study generates new research data: PXRD diffractograms, DSC thermograms and FTIR spectra of the polymer–ibuprofen solid dispersions, plus UV-vis dissolution profiles, all measured in triplicate. From these the authors derive crystallinity values and calculate solubility and Flory–Huggins parameters. These are measurements from laboratory experiments, which the criteria explicitly count as research data, and the paper confirms the data are in the article and its supplementary material (D1). The paper names three software packages: EVA (PXRD background removal), TA Universal Analysis (DSC enthalpy integration) and OMNIC (FTIR spectral analysis). All are standard instrument software used only to process the instruments’ output, so they count as utility use rather than research software (S3). The CRediT statement credits two authors with “software”, but no software is described or claimed as a contribution, so this isn’t enough evidence for S1. Under a stricter reading that treats instrument software as research software, the grade would be S2D1.

S3D3. No research software is used or built. The paper is a historical close reading of archival sources such as letters, committee minutes, the exhibition catalogue and photographs. Each source is cited individually and never assembled or analysed as a dataset, so it doesn’t count as using research data (D2). No new data is collected either (D1).
Agreed.

It’s D1 because the authors made the compound, collected new X-ray diffraction data and solved a new crystal structure, which they deposited with the CCDC (1537099). It’s S2 because, although no new software is claimed, the paper names SHELXT and SHELXL for solving and refining the structure, along with APEX3, SAINT, SADABS and DIAMOND. SHELXT and SHELXL are crystallography programs built for research, not generic tools like Excel,

D1: The authors collected new qualitative data: seven interviews (three focus groups and four one-to-one semi-structured interviews) with 22 teachers. They recorded the interviews and transcribed them word for word. Interview transcripts count as research data under the criteria, and these were created in this study, so D1.

S3: The transcripts were coded and themes grouped in NVivo, a commercial, general-purpose package for qualitative data analysis. It’s comparable to the generic statistical and data-processing software that the criteria exclude from research software. NVivo is mentioned once, in passing, as a tool for organising codes. The authors did the theme finding and the mapping onto the Activity Theory framework themselves. No software is claimed as a contribution, and none was created or extended, so this is software used as a utility: S3.

Note: The same paper could be graded S2D1 if qualitative data analysis software like NVivo is treated as research software, because it was used for substantive analysis. The criteria don’t settle this yet. It’s worth adding as an edge case.

S3D3. This is a narrative review: it summarises published work on protein–ionic liquid interactions and reports no original research. It has no methods section or systematic search strategy. The authors don’t claim to have created or used research software, and the computational work it discusses (COSMO-RS screening, MD simulations) was done by other cited groups. No research data is generated or used either. Tables 1–5 compile values from the literature, but they’re selected, cited summaries of earlier papers rather than a dataset built by systematic extraction, and the criteria exclude literature and reviews of literature from research data.

S3D1. Software (S3): The paper doesn’t mention any research software. The analysis is described as manual interpretive content analysis following Miles and Huberman, with no tools named. Data (D1): The authors report collecting new data through seven years of fieldwork (2007–2014): 25 interviews, non-participant observations, and archival research. The paper doesn’t say the interviews were recorded or transcribed. However, it reproduces long verbatim quotes from named interviewees in Tables 1–4, which wouldn’t be possible without a record of the interviews. The authors also call this material “data” and say they analysed it. It also matches the criteria’s examples of research data (“interview transcripts”, “observations from fieldwork”). They also used existing archival and secondary data, which on its own would be D2, but generated takes precedence over used. If verbatim quotes aren’t accepted as evidence of recorded data, the grade falls back to S3D2, not S3D3.

S1D1. New measurements (PL spectra, g²(τ) correlations and ODMR spectra) are collected on a home-built confocal microscopy setup, and the paper states that “the datasets generated as part of the current study” are available on request (D1). The authors implement their own spin Hamiltonian simulations and a three-level kinetic model to interpret the ODMR results, and the code availability statement confirms the analysis codes are held by the corresponding authors and available on request (S1).
